docs.title: Advanced Higher Computing Science
docs.text:
Welcome to Advanced Higher Computing Science.

Advanced Higher Computing Science is the most challenging school-level Computing Science qualification offered by the SQA. The course develops advanced problem-solving, analytical thinking, software development, database design and web development skills. It provides excellent preparation for university courses in Computing Science, Software Engineering, Cyber Security, Data Science and related disciplines.

Throughout the course, you will learn how to analyse complex problems, design effective solutions, implement those solutions using programming techniques, and evaluate the effectiveness of your work. You will also develop independent learning and project management skills through the completion of a substantial practical project.

docs.title: Course Structure
docs.text:
The course is organised into four main areas:

Area Description Software Design and Development Advanced programming concepts, algorithms, data structures, object-oriented programming, testing and evaluation. Database Design and Development Database analysis, design, implementation, SQL and data management. Web Design and Development Design and development of interactive websites using web technologies. Computer Systems Computer architecture, networking, operating systems and emerging technologies.

Analysis, design, implementation, testing and evaluation skills are developed throughout the course and applied across multiple contexts.

docs.text:
The final examination lasts 2 hours and assesses knowledge, understanding and problem-solving skills from across the course.

The question paper contains:

  • A mandatory Software Design and Development section
  • Optional sections covering Database Design and Development and Web Design and Development
  • Questions requiring analysis, design, evaluation and application of computing concepts

Advanced Higher Computing Science is highly regarded by universities and employers because it develops both theoretical understanding and practical problem-solving skills that are essential within the computing industry.

docs.title: Feasibility Studies
docs.text:
What you Need to Know

Describe, exemplify, and implement research for:

  • feasibility studies:
    • economic
    • time
    • legal
    • technical
    • user surveys

Before starting a new system, it’s important to decide if it’s worth the time and money.

This is where a feasibility study comes in as it helps determine:

  • Is the project realistic?
  • Can it be achieved within time and budget?
  • Will it meet the goals set in the problem definition?

A feasibility study should:

  • Be low-cost and quick to complete

  • Involve no legal commitment to proceed

  • Suggest options or alternatives

  • End with a clear report for the client, showing:

    • Costs
    • Benefits
    • Possible solutions
    • Recommendations

Key Points

  • The feasibility study should be conducted relatively cheaply and within a fairly short time frame.

  • There are no legal or contractual requirements at this stage.

  • The findings of the feasibility study are presented to the client in the form of a report.

  • This report indicates costs, benefits, alternatives and appropriate recommendations.

docs.title: Feasibility Studies
docs.text: A feasibility study should look at the following five main areas:

docs.title: Economic Feasibility
docs.text:
💷 What is Economic Feasibility?

Economic Feasibility deals with the cost implications involved.

Management will want to know how much each option will cost, what is affordable within the company’s budget and what they get for their money.

Economic feasibility asks:

Can we afford this system, and is it worth it?

A system is economically feasible if:

  • Its benefits outweigh the costs

  • It reaches break-even within a realistic timeframe

Example:

A school wants a new timetable system. If the software costs £10,000 but saves £15,000 in admin time over a year, then it’s economically feasible.

docs.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis
docs.text:
A cost-benefit-analysis is part of the budgetary feasibility study.

If the project is not cost-effective then there is no point proceeding. Setting up a new computer system is an investment and involves capital outlay.

The costs of a new system include:

  • the costs of acquiring it in the first place (consultancy fees, program development including cost of any resources required for development, etc.)

  • the costs of installing it (disruption of current operations, cost of new equipment, alteration of workplace, etc.)

  • the costs of maintaining it which also includes training.

In the long term, management will also want to know the ‘break-even point’ when the new system stops costing money and starts to make money.

Economic Feasibility is Difficult to Estimate

It's often difficult to accurately calculate future costs and benefits.

Estimations depend heavily on the expertise and experience of the systems analyst.

Once the system begins to generate value, it's important to distinguish the types of benefits it brings. These can be divided into two categories: tangible(something you can see, touch, or easily quantify) and intangible(something that is not easily measured or quantified).

Benefits generated by a system can be tangible or intangible, as shown below:

| Tangible Benefits | Intangible Benefits | |--------------------------|-----------------------------| | Reduced running costs | Improved staff morale | | Increased operational speed| Better customer perception | | Increased throughput | Easier communication | | Better reporting facilities| Increased job satisfaction | 🚨 Note: __Not all the costs and benefits lend themselves to direct measurement__.

Key Points

  • The client will want to know the cost of each option and what they get for their money.

  • A system is only economically feasible if the benefits of the development outweigh the costs. For this reason a cost benefit analysis is carried out.

docs.title: Time Feasibility
docs.text:
⏱️ What is Time Feasibility?

Time feasibility asks: Can the system be developed and implemented within the available time, and will it be ready when it is needed? It considers:

The time needed for development, installation, and training

The effect on the client’s schedule or operations

Example

A school wants to install a new report-writing system in time for the October break. If development, testing, and training will take 4 months and it’s already July, the project may not be time feasible.

If the project can be completed within a realistic timeframe and without disrupting important business operations, it is considered time feasible.

docs.title: Factors That Affect Time Feasibility
docs.text:
• Total time required for system development
  • Client’s calendar — busy periods, deadlines, seasonal events
  • When installation and training can take place
  • When the system must be fully operational
  • Availability of staff and resources

docs.title: Questions to Ask
docs.text:
• How long will the system take to develop?
  • When is the least disruptive time to install it?
  • Will it be ready by the required date?

🚨 Note: A system can be technically and economically feasible but still not time feasible if it won’t be finished in time to be useful. Delays can make the system pointless or even harmful to the organisation.

Key Points

  • Time feasibility focuses on scheduling and deadlines

  • A system must be ready when the client needs it.

  • Development, training, and installation must fit within the timeline.

  • Failing to meet the deadline can make the system unusable, even if it works perfectly

docs.title: Legal Feasibility
docs.text:
Legal feasibility is about ensuring the proposed system complies with all relevant laws and regulations. Organisations must assess any legal risks that may arise from developing, deploying, or using the system.

⚖️ What is Legal Feasibility?

Legal feasibility considers whether the new system complies with relevant laws and regulations, including:

  • Contracts and liability: Will the system change responsibilities under existing contracts?
  • Health and safety: Will it meet workplace and digital safety standards?
  • Data protection laws (e.g. GDPR): Will it handle personal data legally and securely?
  • International regulations: Will it comply with laws in other countries where users or data may reside (e.g. EU, USA)?
  • Software licensing: Are appropriate licenses available and affordable?

Software Licensing Considerations

Software licensing can be complex and must be carefully checked. The organisation must ensure that:

  • The right type of licence is used:
  • Client licence (per seat)
  • Server licence
  • Network licence

  • Site licence

  • The licence duration is appropriate:

  • Annual subscription
  • Perpetual (one-off) purchase

Different vendors have different rules, so licensing terms should be verified before proceeding.

docs.title: Technical Feasibility
docs.text:
Technical feasibility examines whether the proposed system can be developed and implemented using available technology, hardware, and expertise. It helps identify whether the organisation has the technical capability or needs additional resources.

🖥️ What is Technical Feasibility?

Technical feasibility assesses whether the system can be built and run using the organisation’s current or accessible technology. It includes:

  • Required hardware and software: Are the necessary tools available or affordable?
  • Technical skills: Do staff or developers have the expertise to implement and maintain the system?
  • Integration: Can the new system work with existing systems?
  • Support and maintenance: Are updates, patches, and technical support available?
  • Hardware specifications: Are existing devices powerful enough?
  • Network capacity: Can the network cope with the new system?
  • Storage requirements: Is sufficient storage available?
  • Software compatibility: Will the new system work with existing software?

Example

If a school wants to run a new multimedia learning platform but only has outdated computers, the system may not be technically feasible unless upgrades are made.

docs.title: User Surveys
docs.text:
In addition to the feasibility study, surveys and questionnaires help gather feedback from users, especially when many opinions are needed. This helps ensure the system meets real needs.

📋 What is a User Study?

User feasibility ensures that the proposed solution aligns with user expectations and requirements, which is essential for the project's success. It helps determine:

  • User needs: Will the system actually solve the users’ problems?
  • Ease of use: Is the system user-friendly and intuitive?
  • User acceptance: Are users willing to adopt the system?
  • Usability challenges: Are there barriers that could prevent adoption?

Here's why user feasibility is important: - It identifies potential roadblocks early, such as usability issues or resistance to change, allowing adjustments to the design or implementation plan. - It ensures the project addresses real user needs, increasing its relevance and value. - It improves the overall user experience by considering preferences and behaviours. - It increases adoption rates – if users find the system easy to use and beneficial, they're more likely to embrace it.

In short, user feasibility isn't just a nice-to-have – it's essential for determining whether a project is practical, usable, and likely to succeed.

For example, a new library system would be developed following some time spent capturing the experience of existing librarians and how they operate.

docs.title: Methods of Gathering User Information
docs.text:
Common methods include:

  • Questionnaires and surveys
  • Interviews
  • Observation
  • Focus groups

Different methods provide different types of information and are often used together during a feasibility study.

The users of a particular program are often best placed to identify problems and suggest improvements based on real experience. If the system is brand new, the target user group should still understand the domain well enough to provide useful input.

When the opinion of a number of users is required, it is often easier to create a survey or questionnaire which will capture the information that the project team require.

Example: A college developing a new library system might survey librarians to ask what features they need most.

docs.title: Summary of Feasibility Studies
docs.text: Feasibility Type Main Question Economic Can we afford it? Time Can it be completed on time? Legal Does it comply with the law? Technical Do we have the technology and expertise? User Surveys Do users want and support the solution?

docs.title: Project Planning
docs.text:
# Project Management

  • AH Analysis - Gantt Charts

docs.title: What is Project Management?
docs.text:
Project management is the process of planning, organising, scheduling and monitoring a project to ensure it is completed successfully.

Effective project management helps ensure that:

  • Deadlines are met
  • Resources are used efficiently
  • Progress can be monitored
  • Problems can be identified early
  • The project remains within its planned timescale and budget

docs.title: What is in a project plan?
docs.text:
The primary aspects of a project plan are:

  1. Tasks/Subtasks
  2. Identify Timescales
  3. Gantt Chart
  4. Identify Budget/Resources

docs.title: Tasks and Deadlines
docs.text:
A project should be broken down into an appropriate set of tasks. Tasks should be broken down into sub tasks. Once subtasks are identified timescales and deadlines will have to be assigned - people work more effectively to deadlines.

Advantages of sub tasks:

  1. Concurrent processes can be identified,
  2. Indication of % complete/tracking progress,
  3. Allow identification of the dependency of tasks on the completion of others.
  4. Critical Path Analysis
  5. Delegation of responsibility for subtasks

docs.title: Concurrent Tasks
docs.text:
Concurrent tasks are tasks that can be carried out at the same time because they do not depend on each other being completed first.

Identifying concurrent tasks can reduce the overall duration of a project and make better use of available resources.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
If a task has a relationship with another task then there may be a dependency between the tasks:

Finish to Start: Activity A must finish before Activity B can begin

Example

A : Foundations Dug

B : Concrete Poured

Finish to Finish: Activity A must be complete before activity B can finish

Example

A : Last chapter written

B (Entire book written)

Start to Start: Activity B can only start after Activity A has started

Start to Finish: Activity B cannot finish before Activity A has finished

Example

A : New shift started

B Previous Shift finish

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Scheduling is the process of allocating tasks to specific time periods and determining when work should be carried out.

A schedule helps project managers to:

  • Estimate project completion dates
  • Allocate resources effectively
  • Identify task dependencies
  • Monitor progress
  • Identify potential delays before they become major problems

When creating a schedule, project managers should consider:

  • Task durations
  • Dependencies between tasks
  • Resource availability
  • Deadlines and milestones
  • Concurrent tasks

Gantt charts are commonly used to represent project schedules visually.

docs.text:

docs.text:
Critical path analysis identifies all tasks that must be complete and their minimum time length.

An extension to any of these tasks would result in the delay of completion of the entire project.

docs.title: Resources and Scheduling
docs.text:
Resources can include access to development tools and end users.

These could be: * Personnel - particularly those with specific skill sets * Physical resources/money/software

Some of these could be available at any time, while others may only be available at certain times.

  • You need to plan to ensure that your project is not held up waiting for resources.
  • Timings should allow for holidays, or other events that affect how much time you can spend on your project.

The tab below in the Gantt project shows the demand placed on particular resources, in this instance they are personnel but resources could be physical resources such as hardware/rooms.

docs.title: Requirement Specifications
docs.text:
A requirement specification helps to:

  • Describe what the system should do.
  • Define the system's functionalities.
  • Provide a basis for system design.
  • Serve as a contract between stakeholders.

docs.title: End-User Requirements
docs.text:
End-user requirements describe what users need from a system in order to complete their tasks successfully.

They are usually written in non-technical language so that clients and users can understand them easily.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
For an online homework submission system:

  • Pupils need to upload homework from home.
  • Teachers need to access submissions from any school computer.
  • Pupils need confirmation that work has been submitted successfully.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The scope defines what is included within a project.

Clearly defining the scope helps prevent unnecessary features being added during development.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Included:

  • Upload homework
  • View feedback
  • Teacher marking

Not Included:

  • Online video lessons
  • Live chat
  • Parent accounts

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
Boundaries define the limits of a system and identify what the system will and will not do.

Clearly defining boundaries helps ensure that development remains focused on the agreed requirements.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Constraints are factors that limit the design or implementation of a solution.

Common constraints include:

  • Budget restrictions
  • Time limitations
  • Available hardware
  • Legal requirements
  • Existing software systems

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements describe the specific behavior or functions of a system.

They detail what the system should do, including tasks, data handling, and interactions.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• The system shall allow pupils to upload homework files.
  • The system shall notify teachers of new submissions.
  • The system shall allow teachers to provide feedback.

docs.title: Identifying Requirements
docs.text:
Requirements can be identified through:

  • Interviews with stakeholders.
  • Questionnaires and surveys.
  • Observation of current systems.
  • Analysis of existing documentation.

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text:
• Pupils can upload homework files.
  • Teachers can access and mark submissions.
  • The system sends confirmation emails upon submission.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Requirement Type Description End-User Requirements What users need from the system Scope What is included in the project Boundaries The limits of the system Constraints Factors that restrict development Functional Requirements What the system must do

docs.title: What is UML?
docs.text:
Unified Modelling Language, often shortened to UML, is a standard way of visually modelling a system.

At Advanced Higher level, UML is used during analysis to show how users interact with a proposed system.

This page focuses on use case diagrams.

A use case diagram shows:

  • The users or external systems that interact with the system
  • The main tasks the system must support
  • The relationships between users and tasks

docs.title: Use Case Diagrams
docs.text:
A use case diagram is used to model the functionality of a system from the point of view of the user.

It does not show program code, database tables or screen layouts.

Instead, it shows what the system must allow different users to do.

Use case diagrams are useful because they help developers understand the main functional requirements of a system.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
An actor is a person, group or external system that interacts with the system.

Actors are shown outside the system boundary.

Examples of actors include:

  • Pupil
  • Teacher
  • Administrator
  • Customer
  • Payment system
  • Email system

Important

An actor is not always a person. It can also be another system that communicates with the system being developed.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
A use case is a task or function that the system must carry out for an actor.

Use cases are usually written as short verb phrases.

Examples include:

  • Log in
  • Upload homework
  • View feedback
  • Search records
  • Add new user
  • Generate report

Use cases should describe what the system does, not how the code works.

docs.title: System Boundary
docs.text:
The system boundary is a box that shows what is included inside the system being developed.

Actors are placed outside the system boundary.

Use cases are placed inside the system boundary.

This helps clearly show the difference between:

  • The system itself
  • The people or external systems that interact with it

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
Relationships show how actors and use cases are connected.

The most common relationship is an association.

An association is shown using a straight line between an actor and a use case.

It means that the actor is involved in that use case.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If a pupil can upload homework, a line would connect:

  • The Pupil actor
  • The Upload homework use case

docs.title: Include and Extend Relationships
docs.text: Some use case diagrams may show extra relationships between use cases.

docs.title: Include
docs.text:
An include relationship is used when one use case always includes another use case.

For example:

  • Submit homework may include Log in

This means the user must log in as part of submitting homework.

docs.title: Extend
docs.text:
An extend relationship is used when one use case may optionally add extra behaviour to another use case.

For example:

  • Apply discount may extend Checkout

This means the discount only happens in some situations.

Keep it Simple

For Advanced Higher analysis, the key focus is being able to identify actors, use cases and relationships clearly.

docs.title: Example Scenario
docs.text:
A school wants an online homework submission system.

The system should allow pupils to upload homework and view feedback. Teachers should be able to view submissions and add feedback. An administrator should be able to manage user accounts.

docs.title: Possible Actors
docs.text: Actor Role Pupil Uploads homework and views feedback Teacher Views submissions and adds feedback Administrator Manages user accounts

docs.text: Mistake Why it is a problem Putting actors inside the system boundary Actors are outside the system Writing use cases as nouns only Use cases should describe actions Including implementation details Use case diagrams show functionality, not code Missing relationships It must be clear which actor uses which function Adding too much detail The diagram should show the main user interactions

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Develop a swimming portal for a swimming coach.

  • The system must allow scheduling for swimming lessons.
  • The system must allow swimmers to view their competition time and results.
  • The system must provide a payment system for individual extra training sessions.

docs.title: Persona
docs.text: Avril is a swimming coach and has a hectic life. Swimming competitions are approaching and, as an instructor, she wants to schedule extra training hours for 15 kids. This should also fit into her extremely hectic work program.

docs.title: User Story
docs.text:
Goals

  • She wants a quick way of booking pupils that require extra lessons.

  • She wants to be able to review available dates quickly on a portable device. She also wants swimmers to log in to the system, make and pay for bookings, edit their details, and view their previous competition time.

docs.title: User Scenario
docs.text:
When Avril receives requests from swimmers for dates they would like extra training, she wishes to use the app to pull up a calendar for the next two months and add a swimmer's name as well as a specific time for their training. She wants the app to alert each swimmer immediately with the scheduled information; each swimmer must then accept or reject the time allocated.

Each swimmer should be given generated login information to use on the system. Using this login information, swimmers will be able to log in to the system, view their upcoming swim meets, add/change their personal details, and view data kept for competition times in each swimming technique. Avril should also be able to view all information entered by each swimmer.

Swimmers can also use the system to pay for each individual extra training session.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Avril requires a swimming portal app urgently, you must design a use case diagram for the above scenario, your diagram should include at least one example for each of the following structures:

a) <<include>>

b) <<extend>>

c) generalization

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Develop a holiday booking App

The system must:

  • maintain a database of trips available
  • Allow users to search for particular locations
  • Allow users to view reviews
  • Allow users to book a particular trip using various payment methods
  • Allow users to change the textual language if they wish to do so.

docs.title: Persona
docs.text: Ben is a new dentist in Aberdeen, he is originally from Spain. He is ecstatic about his new job and looking forward to getting to know Scotland.

docs.title: User Story
docs.text:
Goals

Ben would love to be able to take his family up to the highlands on holiday he wishes to book a hotel and transportation on any digital device. He would also really like the information translated to Spanish.

docs.title: User Scenario
docs.text: Ben will like an app he can use to book the trip for his family. He wishes to be able to search for most popular locations in the Highlands. He also wants to select Spanish for language translation, and the ability to use the app to compare prices and reviews posted by other users. Finally, Ben wants to be able to selects the number of travellers, date and use various payment methods (credit card, debit card or wire transfer) details to pay for the trip.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
The travel company wants to develop this app so it can be accessible to busy people like Ben. You have been tasked to design a use case diagram for the above scenario. Include examples of each of these constructs in your diagram:

a) <<include>>

b) <<extend>>

c) Use case generalization

HINT: you will find the Spanish language translation tricky as it is unclear whether you have to develop this yourself or interact with another actor e.g. Google Translate.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Develop an additional module for a school management information system (MIS)

The system must:

  • Allow the Senior Leadership Team (SLT) to browse for available teachers within periods
  • Generate absence reports
  • System must receive and/or notify teachers for cover requests
  • Allow teachers update result and attendance data for pupils
  • Allow SLT to view exam results and attendance data.

docs.title: Persona
docs.text: Eileen is a new deputy head teacher; she has just been promoted to the job and is very enthusiastic about taking the role. She is looking forward to getting to know the teachers and pupils in the new school.

docs.title: User Story
docs.text:
Goals

To assist with the responsibilities of her new role Eileen wishes to have additional functionality added to the school’s management information system (MIS) application to organise cover for classes due to teacher absences. She also wants to be able view the number of classes each teacher has covered. She wants a system in which she can count and view each individual pupil’s absences, and termly results and prelim exam mark.

docs.title: User Scenario
docs.text:
Eileen wants an additional module added to the school’s management information system which can be used for generating necessary reports. She wants the ability to be able to receive cover requests from teachers; search for available teachers for cover within that period/ lesson as well as receive future cover requests for up to 2 months. Eileen wants to count the number of cover each available teacher has completed to date so she can select teachers with the lowest numbers. Eileen wants to receive alerts from teachers requesting absence reports for a pupil. She wants to use the system to search for the pupil and retrieve the absence reports for those specific dates.

Eileen also wishes to use the system to search for pupils’ exam and prelim reports. The system should identify any omissions within the results and notify the subject teachers requesting these results. Teachers should also be able to update results in the system.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Design a use case diagram for the schools MIS, Include these constructs in your diagram:

a) <<include>>

docs.title: Parallel 1D Arrays
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement parallel one-dimensional arrays.

docs.title: What Are Parallel Arrays?
docs.text:
Parallel arrays are two or more 1D arrays in which values at the same index are related.

Pupil Names and Marks
pupil_names = ["Peter", "Laura", "Marie"]
pupil_marks = [20, 21, 23]
Index pupil_names pupil_marks 0 Peter 20 1 Laura 21 2 Marie 23

Peter's name and mark are both at index 0. Marie's details are both at index 2.

Keep the Arrays in Step

The arrays must have the same length, and their values must remain in matching positions. If one array is reordered, the corresponding elements in every parallel array must also move.

docs.title: Accessing Related Values
docs.text:
Use the same index with each array:

Display One Pupil
index = 2

print("Name:", pupil_names[index])
print("Mark:", pupil_marks[index])

docs.title: Processing Parallel Arrays
docs.text:
An index-controlled loop allows the program to access matching elements:

Display All Pupils
for index in range(len(pupil_names)):
    print(pupil_names[index], pupil_marks[index])

Before processing, the program can check that the arrays have matching lengths:

if len(pupil_names) == len(pupil_marks):
    for index in range(len(pupil_names)):
        print(pupil_names[index], pupil_marks[index])
else:
    print("The parallel arrays do not match.")

docs.title: Reading Parallel Data from a CSV File
docs.text:
Suppose School-Reg.csv contains:

Peter,17,R1
Laura,16,R2
Marie,17,R1
Load Parallel Arrays
names = []
ages = []
registration_groups = []

with open("School-Reg.csv", "r") as file:
    for line in file:
        data = line.strip().split(",")

        names.append(data[0])
        ages.append(int(data[1]))
        registration_groups.append(data[2])

for index in range(len(names)):
    print(names[index], ages[index], registration_groups[index])

The age is converted to an integer as it is loaded. The with statement closes the file automatically.

docs.title: Choosing an Appropriate Structure
docs.text:
Parallel arrays are valid when a problem requires them, but they become difficult to manage as more related fields are added. A record keeps all the data for one entity together and is often a clearer solution.

Next: Records

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement records.

docs.title: What Is a Record?
docs.text:
A record stores several related fields about one entity. Its fields can have different data types.

For example, one pupil record could contain:

Field Data type Example name String "Peter" age Integer 17 registration_group String "R1"

This differs from an array, whose elements normally represent values of the same type and purpose.

docs.title: Defining a Record in Python
docs.text:
Python does not have a separate record keyword. A dataclass provides a clear way to define a record-like structure.

Define a Pupil Record
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    age: int
    registration_group: str

The definition specifies the name and data type of every field.

Records and Objects

Python implements this record using a class, but it is being used only to group data. Object-oriented classes containing constructors, private properties and methods are introduced later in the course.

docs.title: Creating a Record
docs.text:
Create One Record
pupil = PupilRecord("Peter", 17, "R1")

The values are supplied in the same order as the fields in the record definition.

docs.title: Accessing Fields
docs.text:
Use dot notation to access an individual field:

Access Record Fields
print(pupil.name)
print(pupil.age)
print(pupil.registration_group)

docs.title: Updating a Field
docs.text:
Update a Record
pupil.registration_group = "R2"
print(pupil.registration_group)

Only the selected field is changed.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
One Pupil Record
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    age: int
    registration_group: str


pupil = PupilRecord("Peter", 17, "R1")
pupil.registration_group = "R2"

print("Name:", pupil.name)
print("Age:", pupil.age)
print("Registration group:", pupil.registration_group)

docs.title: Why Use a Record?
docs.text:
A record:

  • keeps related fields together
  • gives each field a meaningful name
  • supports different data types
  • is easier to maintain than several separate variables

One record stores one entity. To store several pupils, use an array of records.

Next: Arrays of Records

docs.title: Arrays of Records
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement arrays of records.

docs.title: What Is an Array of Records?
docs.text:
An array of records is a one-dimensional array in which every element is a complete record.

Index 0 → one complete pupil record
Index 1 → one complete pupil record
Index 2 → one complete pupil record

Unlike parallel arrays, all fields belonging to one pupil remain together.

docs.title: Creating an Array of Records
docs.text:
Create Pupil Records
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    age: int
    registration_group: str


pupils = [
    PupilRecord("Peter", 17, "R1"),
    PupilRecord("Laura", 16, "R2"),
    PupilRecord("Marie", 17, "R1")
]

The array has three elements. Each element contains the three fields defined by PupilRecord.

docs.title: Accessing and Updating Records
docs.text:
First use an array index to select the record, then use dot notation to select its field:

Access and Update Fields
print(pupils[1].name)  # Laura
print(pupils[1].age)   # 16

pupils[1].registration_group = "R3"

docs.title: Traversing an Array of Records
docs.text:
Display Every Record
for pupil in pupils:
    print(pupil.name, pupil.age, pupil.registration_group)

Only one loop is required because the array itself is one-dimensional.

docs.title: Inputting Records
docs.text:
Input Three Pupil Records
pupils = []

for count in range(3):
    name = input("Enter name: ")
    age = int(input("Enter age: "))
    registration_group = input("Enter registration group: ")

    new_pupil = PupilRecord(name, age, registration_group)
    pupils.append(new_pupil)

Each pass creates one complete record and appends it to the array.

docs.title: Records and Standard Algorithms
docs.text: Later in the course, the whole record can be moved during a sort or returned from a search. The algorithm compares one selected field, such as name or age, while keeping the complete record together.

docs.title: Parallel Arrays Compared with Arrays of Records
docs.text:
Parallel arrays Array of records Related data is split across several arrays Related data is kept in one record Matching indexes must remain synchronised The complete record moves as one element Becomes harder to manage as fields are added Easier to extend with additional fields

Next: Two-Dimensional Arrays

docs.title: Two-Dimensional Arrays
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

For Advanced Higher Computing Science, you should be able to:

  • describe and exemplify a two-dimensional array
  • declare and initialise a two-dimensional array
  • access and update an individual element
  • traverse rows and columns using nested loops
  • process data stored in a two-dimensional array
  • add rows and columns when using Python lists

docs.title: What Is a Two-Dimensional Array?
docs.text:
A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns. It can be pictured as a table, grid or spreadsheet. Every value is an element, located using a row index and a column index.

Python uses lists to represent arrays. A two-dimensional array is therefore a list containing other lists.

A 3 × 4 Seating Plan
classroom = [
    ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David"],
    ["Eve", "Frank", "Grace", "Hannah"],
    ["Ian", "Jack", "Katie", "Liam"]
]
Column 0 Column 1 Column 2 Column 3 Row 0 Alice Bob Charlie David Row 1 Eve Frank Grace Hannah Row 2 Ian Jack Katie Liam

Indexes Start at Zero

classroom[1][2] stores "Grace", because Grace is in row index 1 and column index 2.

docs.title: Why Use a Two-Dimensional Array?
docs.text:
Storing each row in a separate variable makes it harder to process the whole data set. A two-dimensional array keeps related values in one structure and allows one algorithm to process every row and column.

Typical uses include game boards, image pixels, seating plans, monthly figures for several branches and distances between locations.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Element One value stored in the array Row A horizontal group of elements Column A vertical group of elements Index A number used to locate an element Nested loop A loop inside another loop Traverse Visit each required element in an array

docs.title: Continue This Topic
docs.text:
• Accessing and updating elements
  • Traversing and processing arrays
  • Adding rows and columns
  • Two-dimensional array tasks

Start with accessing and updating elements.

docs.title: Accessing an Element
docs.text:
Use two pairs of square brackets: array_name[row_index][column_index].

Accessing Individual Elements
classroom = [
    ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David"],
    ["Eve", "Frank", "Grace", "Hannah"],
    ["Ian", "Jack", "Katie", "Liam"]
]

print(classroom[0][0])  # Alice
print(classroom[1][2])  # Grace
print(classroom[2][3])  # Liam

One index returns a complete row: print(classroom[1]).

docs.title: Updating an Element
docs.text:
Changing a Seat
classroom[2][3] = "Lucas"
print(classroom[2][3])  # Lucas

Only the element at row 2, column 3 changes.

docs.title: Finding the Dimensions
docs.text:
Array Dimensions
number_of_rows = len(classroom)
number_of_columns = len(classroom[0])

print(number_of_rows)     # 3
print(number_of_columns)  # 4

Avoid Invalid Indexes

For a 3 × 4 array, valid row indexes are 0 to 2 and valid column indexes are 0 to 3. An index outside these ranges causes an IndexError.

docs.title: Worked Example: Updating a Game Board
docs.text:
Place a Counter
board = [["-", "-", "-"], ["-", "-", "-"], ["-", "-", "-"]]

row = int(input("Enter row (0-2): "))
column = int(input("Enter column (0-2): "))

if 0 <= row < len(board) and 0 <= column < len(board[row]):
    board[row][column] = "X"
else:
    print("That position is outside the board.")

Next: Traversing and Processing

docs.title: Traversing and Processing 2D Arrays
docs.text: To traverse an array means to visit its elements. A two-dimensional array normally requires a nested loop.

docs.title: Traversing by Value
Traversing by Index
docs.text:
Use indexes when an algorithm must know or change a position.

Display Positions and Values
for row in range(len(classroom)):
    for column in range(len(classroom[row])):
        print(row, column, classroom[row][column])

docs.title: Calculating a Total and Average
docs.text:
Average of All Marks
marks = [[72, 68, 75], [81, 79, 84], [63, 70, 66]]
total = 0
number_of_marks = 0

for row in marks:
    for mark in row:
        total += mark
        number_of_marks += 1

average = total / number_of_marks
print(f"Average: {average:.1f}")

docs.title: Calculating Each Row Total
docs.text:
Total for Each Pupil
for row in range(len(marks)):
    row_total = 0
    for column in range(len(marks[row])):
        row_total += marks[row][column]
    print(f"Pupil {row + 1}: {row_total}")

The row_total must be reset at the start of every new row.

Next: Adding Rows and Columns

docs.title: Adding Rows and Columns
docs.text: Python lists can change size while a program runs.

docs.title: Adding a New Row
docs.text:
Append another list to the outer list:

Append a Row
classroom = [
    ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David"],
    ["Eve", "Frank", "Grace", "Hannah"],
    ["Ian", "Jack", "Katie", "Liam"]
]

classroom.append(["Maya", "Noah", "Olivia", "Paul"])

The new row should normally contain the same number of elements as the existing rows.

docs.title: Adding a New Column
docs.text:
A column is spread across all rows, so append one value to each inner list:

Append an Empty Seat to Every Row
for row in classroom:
    row.append("")

To add different values:

Append Different Values
new_column = ["Rory", "Sara", "Tariq", "Uma"]

if len(new_column) == len(classroom):
    for row in range(len(classroom)):
        classroom[row].append(new_column[row])
else:
    print("The column must contain one value for every row.")

docs.title: Creating an Empty Grid
docs.text:
Create a 4 × 5 Grid
grid = []

for row in range(4):
    new_row = []
    for column in range(5):
        new_row.append(0)
    grid.append(new_row)

A Common Python Trap

Avoid [[0] * 5] * 4. Its rows refer to the same inner list, so changing one row can unexpectedly change the others. A concise safe alternative is [[0 for column in range(5)] for row in range(4)].

docs.title: Irregular Arrays
docs.text:
Python permits rows of different lengths. When processing them, use len(array[row]) for the current row instead of assuming every row has the same number of columns.

Complete the tasks in order. Each builds on the previous pages.

Recording Your Work

Your program should:

Run and test your program, then add a printscreen of your code and output to your workbook. Your output should demonstrate a seat being booked.

Write a program that calculates and displays:

  • the total rainfall for all towns and weeks

Run and test your program, then add a printscreen of your code and all four results to your workbook.

Next: Classes and Objects

docs.title: Classes and Objects
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement:

  • classes
  • objects
  • properties
  • methods
  • instantiation

docs.title: From Records to Objects
docs.text:
At Higher, you learned that a record stores all the data about one pupil together. In Python, you may have accessed its fields like this:

print(pupil_record.name)
print(pupil_record.age)
print(pupil_record.registration_group)

The complete record represented one pupil. name, age and registration_group were individual fields inside it.

Object-oriented programming starts with a similar idea. It keeps the information about one pupil together, but uses some new terminology:

Records Object-oriented programming A record structure defines the fields A class defines the properties and methods One record stores data about one pupil One object represents one pupil A field stores one item of data A property stores one item of data

The important new feature is that a class can also define methods. A method is code that performs an action using an object's properties.

docs.title: Four Ideas to Keep Separate
docs.text:
Consider a program that stores pupils.

The short Python examples below preview the four ideas. The syntax is broken down carefully in the numbered steps that follow.

docs.title: Class
docs.text:
Pupil is the class. It defines what every pupil object will store and what every pupil object will be able to do.

First, picture the class as a simple structure:

Pupil class
├── property: name
├── property: year_group
└── method: display_details()

The same structure can then be implemented in Python:

class Pupil:

    def __init__(self, name, year_group):
        self.name = name
        self.year_group = year_group

    def display_details(self):
        print(self.name, self.year_group)
Tree Python property: name self.name property: year_group self.year_group method: display_details() def display_details(self):

The class is the definition. It does not represent a particular pupil.

docs.title: Object
docs.text:
An object is one particular pupil created using the class.

pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)

pupil1 refers to the complete object—not just its name or year group.

docs.title: Property
docs.text:
A property is one item of data stored inside an object.

print(pupil1.name)        # Alice
print(pupil1.year_group)  # 6

The object is pupil1. Its properties are name and year_group.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
A method is an action defined by the class and performed through an object. For example, display_details() can display that object's properties.

pupil1.display_details()

The four terms therefore describe different things:

Term In the pupil example Class The definition called Pupil Object One complete pupil, such as pupil1 Property One value inside the object, such as name Method An action, such as display_details()

docs.title: One Class Can Create Several Objects
docs.text:
The Pupil class can be used to create several separate pupil objects:

pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)
pupil2 = Pupil("Ben", 5)
pupil3 = Pupil("Cara", 6)

Each object follows the same class definition, but stores its own property values.

docs.title: Step 1 — Defining a Class with __init__
docs.text:
Add an Initialiser
class Pupil:

    def __init__(self, name, year_group):
        self.name = name
        self.year_group = year_group

class Pupil: begins the class definition. The indented code underneath belongs to the class.

__init__ is a special method that runs automatically when a new object is created. Its job is to give the new object its initial state.

The name has two underscores before and after init:

__init__

It is commonly pronounced “dunder init”, meaning “double-underscore init”. You do not normally call it directly; Python calls it during instantiation.

Initialiser and Constructor

__init__ is commonly called a constructor in introductory Python. More precisely, it initialises an object after Python has created it.

docs.title: Step 2 — Understanding self
docs.text:
self refers to the particular object currently using the method.

self.name = name

The two uses of name have different jobs:

Code Meaning name A parameter containing a value supplied to __init__ self.name A property stored permanently inside this particular object

The assignment copies the parameter value into the object's property.

parameter                    object property
   name      ──────────────▶    self.name

The same happens here:

self.year_group = year_group

Each object receives its own name and year_group properties.

Is self a Keyword?

self is not a reserved Python keyword, but it is the standard name used for the current object. Using a different name would be confusing and should be avoided.

docs.title: Step 3 — Instantiating an Object
docs.text:
Instantiation means creating an object from a class.

Create One Object
pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)

This statement causes Python to:

  1. create a new Pupil object
  2. call its __init__ method automatically
  3. pass "Alice" into the name parameter
  4. pass 6 into the year_group parameter
  5. store the completed object in pupil1

Although __init__ declares three parameters, only two arguments are written when the object is created:

def __init__(self, name, year_group):
    ...

pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)

Python supplies self automatically. In this call, self refers to the new object that will be stored in pupil1.

Parameter Value received self The new Pupil object—supplied automatically name "Alice" year_group 6

docs.title: Step 4 — Creating Multiple Objects
docs.text:
Create Separate Objects
pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)
pupil2 = Pupil("Ben", 5)

Both objects follow the same class definition, but each has its own data:

Object name year_group pupil1 Alice 6 pupil2 Ben 5

Changing one object does not change the other:

pupil1.year_group = 7

print(pupil1.year_group)  # 7
print(pupil2.year_group)  # 5

docs.title: Step 5 — Accessing Properties
docs.text:
Use dot notation to access a property:

Access Object Properties
print(pupil1.name)
print(pupil1.year_group)

object.property
pupil1.name

The dot separates the object name from the property being accessed.

docs.title: Step 6 — Adding a Method
docs.text:
A method is a subprogram defined inside a class. It describes behaviour belonging to the objects created from that class.

A Class with a Method
class Pupil:

    def __init__(self, name, year_group):
        self.name = name
        self.year_group = year_group

    def display_details(self):
        print("Name:", self.name)
        print("Year group:", self.year_group)

display_details() has a self parameter because it needs to access the properties of the object that calls it.

Call the method using dot notation:

Call an Object Method
pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)
pupil1.display_details()

Python automatically passes pupil1 into the method as self. Conceptually, the call behaves like:

Pupil.display_details(pupil1)

You should normally use the clearer dot-notation version:

pupil1.display_details()

docs.title: How self Selects the Correct Object
docs.text:
The Same Method, Different Objects
pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)
pupil2 = Pupil("Ben", 5)

pupil1.display_details()
pupil2.display_details()

During the first call, self refers to pupil1, so the method displays Alice's properties. During the second call, self refers to pupil2, so it displays Ben's properties.

The method is written once but works with whichever object calls it.

docs.title: Complete Working Example
docs.text:
Pupil Class and Objects
class Pupil:

    def __init__(self, name, year_group):
        self.name = name
        self.year_group = year_group

    def display_details(self):
        print("Name:", self.name)
        print("Year group:", self.year_group)


pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)
pupil2 = Pupil("Ben", 5)

pupil1.display_details()
print()
pupil2.display_details()

Output:

Name: Alice
Year group: 6

Name: Ben
Year group: 5

docs.title: Missing self from a Method Definition
docs.text:
# Incorrect
def display_details():
    print(self.name)

Instance methods must declare self as their first parameter:

# Correct
def display_details(self):
    print(self.name)

docs.title: Forgetting self. When Creating a Property
docs.text:
# This creates only a temporary local variable.
name = name

To store the value in the object, use:

self.name = name

docs.title: Calling a Method Without Parentheses
docs.text:
# Refers to the method but does not call it.
pupil1.display_details

# Calls the method.
pupil1.display_details()

docs.title: Supplying the Wrong Number of Arguments
docs.text:
# Missing the year_group argument.
pupil1 = Pupil("Alice")

The arguments supplied during instantiation must match the parameters declared after self in __init__.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Class A definition or blueprint used to create objects Object One instance of a class Property Data stored in an object Method A subprogram defined inside a class Instantiation Creating an object from a class __init__ Special method that initialises a new object self A reference to the object currently using a method Dot notation Syntax used to access an object's properties and methods

Game Character

    def __init__(self, username, health):

    def display_status(self):

player1 = GameCharacter("SkyRunner", 100)
player1.display_status()

  1. Identify the class, object, properties and method used in the program.
  2. Explain the purpose of __init__ in this program.

Next: Encapsulation

docs.title: Encapsulation
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement encapsulation using public and private properties.

docs.title: Building on Classes and Objects
docs.text:
You have already created objects containing properties and methods:

pupil1.name
pupil1.display_details()

So far, external code has been able to change every property directly. This can allow invalid data to enter an object.

pupil1.attendance = 150

An attendance percentage of 150 is invalid. Encapsulation lets the class control how important properties are accessed and changed.

docs.title: The Main Idea
docs.text:
Picture the class as a boundary around its data and methods:

Pupil object
├── public property: name
├── private property: attendance
├── method: get_attendance()
└── method: set_attendance()

The same structure in Python is:

class Pupil:

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.__attendance = 0

    def get_attendance(self):
        return self.__attendance

    def set_attendance(self, attendance):
        if 0 <= attendance <= 100:
            self.__attendance = attendance
Conceptual view Python Public property name self.name Private property attendance self.__attendance Accessor method get_attendance() Mutator method set_attendance()

docs.title: Public and Private Properties
docs.text:
A public property can be accessed directly from outside the class:

print(pupil1.name)
pupil1.name = "Alicia"

A private property should be accessed only through methods provided by the class.

In Python, a double underscore triggers name mangling:

self.__attendance

This models the private properties used in the SQA reference language and discourages direct external access. Python does not enforce absolute privacy.

docs.title: Accessor Methods
docs.text:
An accessor, sometimes called a getter, returns the value of a private property:

def get_attendance(self):
    return self.__attendance

Use it through an object:

print(pupil1.get_attendance())

When the method runs, self refers to pupil1.

docs.title: Mutator Methods
docs.text:
A mutator, sometimes called a setter, controls changes to a private property:

def set_attendance(self, attendance):
    if 0 <= attendance <= 100:
        self.__attendance = attendance
    else:
        print("Attendance must be between 0 and 100.")

The parameter is checked before the property is changed.

pupil1.set_attendance(95)   # Accepted
pupil1.set_attendance(120)  # Rejected

docs.title: Complete Working Example
Why Use Encapsulation?
docs.text:
Encapsulation:

  • protects properties from accidental changes
  • allows validation before a value is stored
  • keeps responsibility for the data inside its class
  • makes a class easier to update and maintain

docs.title: Updating the Private Property Directly
docs.text:
# Avoid this
pupil1.__attendance = 95

# Use the mutator
pupil1.set_attendance(95)

docs.title: Validating After Storing the Value
docs.text: The value should be checked before it is assigned to the property.

docs.title: Forgetting to Return from an Accessor
docs.text:
def get_attendance(self):
    return self.__attendance

Without return, the caller receives None.

Next: Inheritance and Subclasses

docs.title: Inheritance and Subclasses
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement superclasses, subclasses and inheritance.

docs.title: The Problem of Repeated Code
docs.text:
Suppose a program needs pupil and teacher objects. Both types of person have a name, so defining them independently repeats code:

class Pupil:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name


class Teacher:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

Inheritance allows shared properties and methods to be defined once in a superclass.

docs.title: The Main Idea
docs.text:
Person superclass
├── property: name
└── method: display_name()
        ▲
        │ inherits
        │
Pupil subclass
└── property: year_group

The same relationship in Python is:

class Person:

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def display_name(self):
        print(self.name)


class Pupil(Person):

    def __init__(self, name, year_group):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.year_group = year_group
Conceptual view Python Superclass class Person: Subclass class Pupil(Person): Call superclass initialiser super().__init__(name) Subclass-only property self.year_group

docs.title: Step 1 — Define the Superclass
docs.text:
The superclass contains features shared by more than one type of object:

class Person:

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def display_name(self):
        print(self.name)

docs.title: Step 2 — Define the Subclass
docs.text:
Write the superclass name in brackets after the subclass name:

class Pupil(Person):
    ...

This means that Pupil inherits the properties and methods defined by Person.

docs.title: Step 3 — Call the Superclass Initialiser
docs.text:
def __init__(self, name, year_group):
    super().__init__(name)
    self.year_group = year_group

super().__init__(name) sends name to the Person initialiser. That initialiser stores it in self.name.

The Pupil initialiser then adds the property needed only by pupils: self.year_group.

docs.title: Step 4 — Create a Subclass Object
docs.text:
pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)

The completed object contains both inherited and subclass properties:

pupil1
├── name: Alice       ← inherited from Person
└── year_group: 6     ← defined by Pupil

docs.title: Step 5 — Use an Inherited Method
docs.text:
pupil1.display_name()

display_name() is not written inside Pupil, but a pupil object can use it because it was inherited from Person.

docs.title: Adding Another Subclass
docs.text:
class Teacher(Person):

    def __init__(self, name, subject):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.subject = subject

Pupil and Teacher both inherit name and display_name() while adding their own specialised properties.

             Person
            /      \
       Pupil        Teacher
   year_group       subject

docs.title: Complete Working Example
Omitting the Superclass Name
docs.text:
# Does not inherit from Person
class Pupil:
    ...

# Inherits from Person
class Pupil(Person):
    ...

docs.title: Forgetting super().__init__()
docs.text: If the superclass initialiser is not called, its properties may not be created.

docs.title: Recreating an Inherited Property
docs.text: Let the superclass initialise shared properties rather than duplicating the assignment in every subclass.

Next: Polymorphism

docs.title: Polymorphism
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement polymorphism.

docs.title: Building on Inheritance
docs.text:
Inheritance allows related subclasses to share properties and methods from a superclass. Sometimes each subclass needs its own version of the same action.

For example, both pupils and teachers can display details, but the details displayed are different.

docs.title: The Main Idea
docs.text:
Person superclass
└── method: display_details()
        ▲
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   │         │
 Pupil     Teacher
 display_  display_
 details() details()

Both subclasses use the same method name, but provide different implementations.

class Pupil(Person):

    def display_details(self):
        print("Pupil:", self.name)


class Teacher(Person):

    def display_details(self):
        print("Teacher:", self.name)

This is polymorphism: the same method call can produce different behaviour depending on the object receiving it.

docs.title: Method Overriding
docs.text:
A subclass overrides a method by defining a new method with the same name as an inherited method.

class Person:

    def display_details(self):
        print("Person:", self.name)

When Pupil defines its own display_details(), a pupil object uses the subclass version instead of the inherited version.

docs.title: The Same Call, Different Behaviour
docs.text:
pupil1.display_details()
teacher1.display_details()

The method call has the same form each time:

object.display_details()

The object's class determines which version runs.

docs.title: Processing Different Objects Together
docs.text:
The benefit becomes clearer when related objects are stored in one array:

people = [pupil1, teacher1]

for person in people:
    person.display_details()

The loop does not need separate selection statements to determine the type of each object. It sends the same message—display_details()—to every object.

docs.title: Complete Working Example
Inheritance Compared with Polymorphism
docs.text: Inheritance Polymorphism Creates a relationship between classes Allows related objects to respond differently Shares properties and methods Uses the same method name with different implementations class Pupil(Person): Each subclass defines display_details()

docs.title: Using Different Method Names
docs.text: Polymorphism requires a shared method name. display_pupil() and display_teacher() are two unrelated calls, not this form of polymorphism.

docs.title: Forgetting to Override the Method
docs.text: If a subclass does not provide its own implementation, it uses the inherited superclass version.

docs.title: Checking Every Object Type Manually
docs.text: Long if statements checking each object's type often defeat the purpose of polymorphism. Call the shared method and allow the object to select its implementation.

Next: Arrays of Objects

docs.title: Arrays of Objects
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement arrays of objects.

docs.title: From One Object to Many
docs.text:
So far, object variables have been created separately:

pupil1 = Pupil("Alice", 6)
pupil2 = Pupil("Ben", 5)
pupil3 = Pupil("Cara", 6)

This becomes difficult to process when a program contains many objects. An array stores them under one name.

docs.title: The Main Idea
docs.text:
pupils array
├── index 0 → Pupil object: Alice, 6
├── index 1 → Pupil object: Ben, 5
└── index 2 → Pupil object: Cara, 6

The same structure in Python is:

pupils = [
    Pupil("Alice", 6),
    Pupil("Ben", 5),
    Pupil("Cara", 6)
]

The array is one-dimensional. Each element is a complete object containing its own properties and methods.

docs.title: Step 1 — Define the Class
docs.text:
class Pupil:

    def __init__(self, name, year_group):
        self.name = name
        self.year_group = year_group

    def display_details(self):
        print(self.name, self.year_group)

The class must be defined before its objects can be created.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create the Array
docs.text:
pupils = [
    Pupil("Alice", 6),
    Pupil("Ben", 5),
    Pupil("Cara", 6)
]

Each call to Pupil(...) creates a separate object and places it in the array.

docs.title: Step 3 — Access an Object
docs.text:
Use an index to select the object:

print(pupils[0])

Use dot notation after the index to select one of that object's properties:

print(pupils[0].name)        # Alice
print(pupils[0].year_group)  # 6

pupils[0].name
   │      └── property
   └───────── object at index 0

docs.title: Step 4 — Update an Object
docs.text:
pupils[1].year_group = 6

This updates the year_group property of the object at index 1.

If the property is private, call its mutator method instead of changing it directly.

docs.title: Step 5 — Call an Object's Method
docs.text:
pupils[2].display_details()

The index selects Cara's object. Python then calls display_details() with that object as self.

docs.title: Step 6 — Traverse the Array
docs.text:
for pupil in pupils:
    pupil.display_details()

On each pass, pupil refers to the next complete object in the array.

docs.title: Adding Another Object
docs.text:
new_pupil = Pupil("David", 5)
pupils.append(new_pupil)

This creates a new object and appends it to the array.

docs.title: Complete Working Example
docs.text:
Process an Array of Pupil Objects

    def __init__(self, name, year_group):
        self.name = name
        self.year_group = year_group

    def display_details(self):
        print("Name:", self.name)
        print("Year group:", self.year_group)


pupils = [
    Pupil("Alice", 6),
    Pupil("Ben", 5),
    Pupil("Cara", 6)
]

pupils[1].year_group = 6
pupils.append(Pupil("David", 5))

for pupil in pupils:
    pupil.display_details()
    print()

docs.title: Arrays of Records Compared with Arrays of Objects
docs.text:
Array of records Array of objects Each element stores fields Each element stores properties and can use methods Used primarily to group data Used to group data and behaviour The record structure defines fields The class defines properties and methods

Both are one-dimensional arrays. Later, a search or sort can compare one field or property while processing the complete record or object.

docs.title: Forgetting the Array Index
docs.text:
# Incorrect: pupils is the array, not one Pupil object
print(pupils.name)

# Correct
print(pupils[0].name)

docs.title: Appending the Class Instead of an Object
docs.text:
# Incorrect
pupils.append(Pupil)

# Correct
pupils.append(Pupil("David", 5))

docs.title: Recreating the Array Inside a Loop
docs.text: Create the array before the loop so earlier objects are not lost.

docs.title: Complete Working Example
docs.text:
This program combines the object-oriented programming concepts from this section:

  • Objects
  • Inheritance
  • Encapsulation
  • Polymorphism

The example uses a school register system with a superclass called Person and two subclasses called Pupil and Teacher.

docs.title: Conceptual View
docs.text:
Read the structure before studying the complete Python program:

Person superclass
├── property: name
└── method: display_details()
        ▲
        │
   ┌────┴─────────┐
   │              │
Pupil          Teacher
├── year_group ├── subject
├── attendance └── display_details()
├── set_attendance()
├── get_attendance()
└── display_details()

The Python program implements this structure using inheritance, encapsulation and polymorphism.

docs.title: Program
docs.text:
# Person is the superclass.
# It stores the data and methods shared by pupils and teachers.
class Person:

    def __init__(self, name):
        # Each person object stores its own name.
        self.name = name

    def display_details(self):
        print("Name:", self.name)


# Pupil is a subclass of Person.
# It inherits the name property from Person.
class Pupil(Person):

    def __init__(self, name, year_group, attendance):
        # Call the constructor from the superclass.
        super().__init__(name)

        # Store data that only pupil objects need.
        self.year_group = year_group

        # Name mangling models a private attendance property.
        self.__attendance = 0

        # Use the method so the attendance value can be validated.
        self.set_attendance(attendance)

    def set_attendance(self, attendance):
        # Only store attendance if it is a valid percentage.
        if 0 <= attendance <= 100:
            self.__attendance = attendance
        else:
            print("Attendance must be between 0 and 100")

    def get_attendance(self):
        # Return the private attendance value.
        return self.__attendance

    def display_details(self):
        # This method overrides display_details() from Person.
        print("Pupil:", self.name)
        print("Year group:", self.year_group)
        print("Attendance:", str(self.__attendance) + "%")


# Teacher is another subclass of Person.
class Teacher(Person):

    def __init__(self, name, subject):
        # Call the constructor from the superclass.
        super().__init__(name)

        # Store data that only teacher objects need.
        self.subject = subject

    def display_details(self):
        # This method also overrides display_details() from Person.
        print("Teacher:", self.name)
        print("Subject:", self.subject)


# Create a list containing different types of objects.
people = [
    Pupil("Alice", 6, 95),
    Teacher("Mrs Smith", "Computing"),
    Pupil("Ben", 5, 88)
]

# The same method call works for both Pupil and Teacher objects.
for person in people:
    person.display_details()
    print()

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Pupil: Alice
Year group: 6
Attendance: 95%

Teacher: Mrs Smith
Subject: Computing

Pupil: Ben
Year group: 5
Attendance: 88%

docs.title: How the Program Uses OOP
docs.text: Concept How it is used Object Each pupil and teacher is created as an object Class Person, Pupil and Teacher define the structure of the objects Inheritance Pupil and Teacher inherit from Person Encapsulation The Pupil class stores attendance as a private property Polymorphism The same display_details() method works differently for pupils and teachers

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This complete example shows how object-oriented programming can be used to model a real-world system.

The program stores related data inside objects and allows different object types to respond to the same method call in their own way.

Next: SQLite with Python

docs.title: SQLite with Python
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement code that:

  • opens and closes a connection to a database
  • executes an SQL query
  • formats query results

docs.title: The Database Programming Sequence
docs.text:
A database program normally follows four steps:

  1. open a connection
  2. create a cursor and execute an SQL statement
  3. process and format any results
  4. close the connection

Python includes the sqlite3 module, so no additional package is required.

docs.title: Opening a Connection
docs.text:
Connect to a Database
import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cursor = connection.cursor()

If school.db does not exist, SQLite creates it. The cursor is used to send SQL statements to the database.

docs.title: Creating a Table
docs.text:
This setup code creates a table for the examples on this page:

Create the Pupil Table
cursor.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pupil (
        pupil_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
        name TEXT NOT NULL,
        age INTEGER NOT NULL,
        registration_group TEXT NOT NULL
    )
""")

connection.commit()

commit() permanently saves a change made by CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.

docs.title: Executing an INSERT Statement
docs.text:
Use placeholders for values supplied by the program:

Insert One Record
name = input("Enter name: ")
age = int(input("Enter age: "))
registration_group = input("Enter registration group: ")

cursor.execute(
    "INSERT INTO pupil (name, age, registration_group) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
    (name, age, registration_group)
)

connection.commit()

Use Parameters

Do not build an SQL statement by joining user input into a string. Placeholders keep data separate from the SQL command and help prevent SQL injection.

docs.title: Retrieving and Formatting Results
docs.text:
Display Query Results
cursor.execute("""
    SELECT pupil_id, name, age, registration_group
    FROM pupil
    ORDER BY name
""")

rows = cursor.fetchall()

for row in rows:
    print(f"ID: {row[0]}")
    print(f"Name: {row[1]}")
    print(f"Age: {row[2]}")
    print(f"Registration group: {row[3]}")
    print()

fetchall() returns the result set as a list of rows. Each field in a row is accessed by its position.

docs.title: A Parameterised SELECT Statement
docs.text:
A one-item tuple requires a trailing comma:

Select One Pupil
target_name = input("Enter a name: ")

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT pupil_id, name, age, registration_group FROM pupil WHERE name = ?",
    (target_name,)
)

row = cursor.fetchone()

if row is None:
    print("Pupil not found.")
else:
    print(row[1], row[2], row[3])

docs.title: Updating and Deleting Data
docs.text:
Update a Record
cursor.execute(
    "UPDATE pupil SET registration_group = ? WHERE pupil_id = ?",
    ("R3", 2)
)
connection.commit()
Delete a Record
cursor.execute("DELETE FROM pupil WHERE pupil_id = ?", (2,))
connection.commit()

docs.title: Storing Results in an Array of Records
docs.text:
Query results can be converted into the record structure studied earlier:

Convert Rows to Records
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    pupil_id: int
    name: str
    age: int
    registration_group: str


cursor.execute("""
    SELECT pupil_id, name, age, registration_group
    FROM pupil
    ORDER BY name
""")

pupils = [PupilRecord(*row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]

for pupil in pupils:
    print(pupil.name, pupil.registration_group)

The order of the selected fields must match the order of the fields in PupilRecord.

docs.title: Closing the Connection
docs.text:
Always close the database connection when it is no longer required:

connection.close()

docs.title: Complete Read-Only Example
docs.text:
Connect, Query, Format and Close
import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
cursor = connection.cursor()

cursor.execute("SELECT name, age FROM pupil ORDER BY name")
rows = cursor.fetchall()

for row in rows:
    print(f"{row[0]} is {row[1]} years old.")

connection.close()

Next: Bubble Sort

docs.title: Bubble Sort
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement bubble sort, and read and explain code that uses it.

docs.title: What Is Bubble Sort?
docs.text:
Bubble sort repeatedly compares neighbouring elements. If they are in the wrong order, it swaps them. After each pass, the largest unsorted value has moved to its correct position at the end of the array.

Bubble Sort a 1D Array
numbers = [7, 2, 5, 3, 4]

for pass_number in range(len(numbers) - 1):
    for index in range(len(numbers) - 1 - pass_number):
        if numbers[index] > numbers[index + 1]:
            temporary = numbers[index]
            numbers[index] = numbers[index + 1]
            numbers[index + 1] = temporary

print(numbers)

Output:

[2, 3, 4, 5, 7]

docs.title: How the Loops Work
docs.text:
• The outer loop controls the passes through the array.
  • The inner loop compares neighbouring elements.
  • pass_number shortens each pass because the values at the end are already sorted.
  • The entire array is sorted when all required passes are complete.

docs.title: Sorting Records
docs.text:
The same algorithm can compare a field in an array of records. When two fields are out of order, the complete records must be swapped.

Bubble Sort Records by Score
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    score: int


pupils = [
    PupilRecord("Anna", 68),
    PupilRecord("Ben", 81),
    PupilRecord("Cara", 74)
]

for pass_number in range(len(pupils) - 1):
    for index in range(len(pupils) - 1 - pass_number):
        if pupils[index].score > pupils[index + 1].score:
            temporary = pupils[index]
            pupils[index] = pupils[index + 1]
            pupils[index + 1] = temporary

for pupil in pupils:
    print(pupil.name, pupil.score)

The algorithm compares the score field but swaps each complete record. The resulting array is ordered by score and is ready for a binary search using that same field.

Next: Insertion Sort

docs.title: Insertion Sort
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement insertion sort, and read and explain code that uses it.

docs.title: What Is Insertion Sort?
docs.text:
Insertion sort builds a sorted section at the beginning of an array. Starting with the second element, it:

  1. stores the current value
  2. shifts larger values in the sorted section one position to the right
  3. inserts the stored value into the gap
  4. repeats for every remaining element

Shift, Then Insert

This implementation shifts elements to make a gap. It does not repeatedly swap neighbouring values like bubble sort.

docs.title: Sorting a 1D Array
docs.text:
Insertion Sort a 1D Array
scores = [7, 2, 5, 3, 4]

for index in range(1, len(scores)):
    current_score = scores[index]
    position = index - 1

    while position >= 0 and scores[position] > current_score:
        scores[position + 1] = scores[position]
        position -= 1

    scores[position + 1] = current_score

print(scores)

Output:

[2, 3, 4, 5, 7]

docs.title: How the Variables Work
docs.text: Variable Purpose index Selects the next element from the unsorted section current_score Temporarily stores the value being inserted position Moves backwards through the sorted section

docs.title: Sorting Parallel Arrays
docs.text:
When parallel arrays are sorted, every corresponding value must move with the sort key:

Sort Parallel Arrays by Score
names = ["Anna", "Ben", "Cara"]
scores = [85, 72, 90]

for index in range(1, len(scores)):
    current_score = scores[index]
    current_name = names[index]
    position = index - 1

    while position >= 0 and scores[position] > current_score:
        scores[position + 1] = scores[position]
        names[position + 1] = names[position]
        position -= 1

    scores[position + 1] = current_score
    names[position + 1] = current_name

for index in range(len(names)):
    print(names[index], scores[index])

docs.title: Sorting an Array of Records
docs.text:
An array of records is easier to manage because each complete record moves as one element:

Sort Records by Score
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class PupilRecord:
    name: str
    score: int


pupils = [
    PupilRecord("Anna", 85),
    PupilRecord("Ben", 72),
    PupilRecord("Cara", 90)
]

for index in range(1, len(pupils)):
    current_pupil = pupils[index]
    position = index - 1

    while position >= 0 and pupils[position].score > current_pupil.score:
        pupils[position + 1] = pupils[position]
        position -= 1

    pupils[position + 1] = current_pupil

for pupil in pupils:
    print(pupil.name, pupil.score)

The score field is compared, but the complete PupilRecord is shifted and inserted.

docs.title: Bubble Sort Compared with Insertion Sort
docs.text:
Bubble sort Insertion sort Repeatedly compares neighbours Compares the current value with the sorted section Swaps values that are out of order Shifts values, then inserts the current value Largest unsorted value moves to the end after a pass Sorted section grows from the beginning

Both algorithms produce sorted data suitable for binary search.
