docs.title: Binary Search
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

Describe, exemplify and implement:

  • Binary search

Read, trace and explain code that uses binary search.

docs.title: What is Binary Search?
docs.text:
Binary search is a searching algorithm that repeatedly divides a sorted list in half until the target value is found.

Unlike a linear search, binary search:

  • Requires the data to be sorted
  • Eliminates half of the remaining values after each comparison
  • Is significantly faster for large datasets

Important

Binary search only works correctly on sorted data.

docs.title: How Binary Search Works
docs.text:
Suppose we want to find the value 23.

[3] [7] [12] [18] [23] [29] [34] [41] [50]
                 ↑
               Middle
  1. Find the middle value.
  2. Compare the middle value with the target.
  3. If the target is smaller, search the left half.
  4. If the target is larger, search the right half.
  5. Repeat until the value is found.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Suppose we want to find the value 34.

[3] [7] [12] [18] [23] [29] [34] [41] [50]

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Middle value = 23

34 is greater than 23, so search the right half.

[29] [34] [41] [50]

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Middle value = 34

Target found.

The search is complete.

docs.title: Why Was 34 Accepted if it Was Not the Middle Value?
docs.text:
A common misunderstanding is that binary search is looking for a value that is always in the middle of the original list.

This is not true.

Binary search repeatedly reduces the search area and then calculates a new middle position.

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Index:  0  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Value: [3][7][12][18][23][29][34][41][50]

The algorithm starts with:

low = 0
high = 8
mid = (low + high) // 2
mid = 4

The middle position is index 4, which contains the value 23.

Since 34 is greater than 23, everything to the left of 23 can be ignored.

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
The remaining search area is:

Index:  5   6   7   8
Value: [29][34][41][50]

Notice that there are now four values remaining.

With an even number of values there is no single middle value.

Binary search solves this problem using integer division (//), which always rounds down.

mid = (5 + 8) // 2
mid = 6

Index 6 contains the value 34.

The target has been found.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Binary search always calculates the middle index, not the middle value.

If there are two possible middle positions, integer division causes the algorithm to choose the lower index.

This guarantees that the search area becomes smaller every time the algorithm runs.

docs.title: Why Must Data Be Sorted?
docs.text:
Binary search works by eliminating half of the remaining data after each comparison.

This is only possible when the data is stored in order.

For example, if the middle value is 23 and the target value is 34, binary search knows that 34 must be to the right of 23.

Without sorted data, this assumption would be incorrect and the algorithm could miss the target value completely.

docs.title: Binary Search of Integers
Trace Table Example
docs.text:
Searching for the value 34:

Low High Mid Value at Mid Action 0 8 4 23 Search right half 5 8 6 34 Found

Trace tables are commonly used to explain how binary search works step by step.

Explanation low and high Store the current search boundaries. mid Stores the middle position. Target Found Return the index immediately. Target Smaller Search the left half of the list. Target Larger Search the right half of the list.

docs.title: Binary Search of Strings
Binary Search of an Array of Records
docs.text:
An array of records is still a one-dimensional sequence. The records must be sorted by the same field that the binary search compares.

Search Records by Name
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Pupil:
    name: str
    score: int


# The records are already sorted by name.
pupils = [
    Pupil("Anna", 68),
    Pupil("Ben", 81),
    Pupil("Cara", 74),
    Pupil("David", 59),
    Pupil("Eilidh", 77)
]


def binary_search_by_name(pupils, target):
    low = 0
    high = len(pupils) - 1

    while low <= high:
        middle = (low + high) // 2

        if pupils[middle].name == target:
            return middle
        elif target < pupils[middle].name:
            high = middle - 1
        else:
            low = middle + 1

    return -1


position = binary_search_by_name(pupils, "Cara")

if position != -1:
    print(pupils[position])
else:
    print("Pupil not found")

The algorithm compares the name field but returns the position of the complete record. If the program searched by score instead, the records would first need to be sorted by score.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Faster than linear search for large datasets
  • Reduces the number of comparisons required
  • Efficient when data is already sorted

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Requires data to be sorted first
  • More complex to implement than linear search
  • Less efficient for very small datasets

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Feature Binary Search Data Sorted Required Method Repeatedly divides data in half Speed Fast for large datasets Complexity More complex than linear search

Binary search completes the algorithm sequence. Bubble sort or insertion sort can prepare unsorted data, provided the sort and search use the same value or record field.

docs.title: Cake Maker
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 3

Save your file as: Cake Maker.py

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
A cake recipe uses 100 grams of flour and 50 grams of sugar for every egg used in the recipe.

Write a program that asks the user how many eggs they want to use, validates the input, then calculates how much flour and sugar are needed.

Validation rules:

  • the number of eggs must be positive
  • the number of eggs must be at least 1
  • the maximum number of eggs is 8

You should assume that the user will always enter an integer.

docs.title: Check Your Program
docs.text: The user should keep being asked to re-enter the number of eggs until they enter a valid number.

Save your file as: Darts.py

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
Create a program that tells a user how many points away from 180 they are after throwing three darts.

The program must check each dart score to make sure it is valid. A single dart cannot score greater than 60.

The user will enter three integers representing each dart.

20
40
5

Example output:

115

docs.title: Check Your Program

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
Design and implement a program that allows the user to enter a positive number.

The program should display all numbers divisible by 5 up to the number entered.

Input: 30

docs.title: Go Kart
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 3

Save your file as: Go Kart.py

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
Write a Python program that estimates the braking distance in metres for a new model of go-kart travelling between 10 and 50 kilometres per hour.

Your program should:

  • keep asking the user to enter a speed until they enter a speed between 10 and 50 inclusive
  • calculate the braking distance in metres by dividing the speed by 5
  • ask the user if the ground is wet
  • expect the user to enter yes if the ground is wet
  • multiply the braking distance by 1.5 if the ground is wet
  • output the final calculated braking distance

Use meaningful variable names, correct syntax and correct indentation.

docs.title: Check Your Program
docs.text: Your program should validate the speed before calculating the braking distance.

docs.title: Ice Cream!
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 3

Save your file as: Ice Cream!.py

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
Write a program that helps an ice cream seller estimate how many ice creams they are likely to sell on a particular day.

Your algorithm should:

  • ask the user to enter whether it is the weekend or a weekday
  • ask the user to enter the temperature forecast in degrees Celsius
  • keep asking for the temperature until the user enters a number between 20 and 45 inclusive
  • calculate the number of ice creams likely to be sold
  • double the estimate if it is a weekend
  • output the estimated number of ice creams likely to be sold

Estimate rules:

  • 100 ice creams are likely to be sold if the temperature is between 20 and 30 degrees inclusive
  • 150 ice creams are likely to be sold if the temperature is between 31 and 38 degrees inclusive
  • 120 ice creams are likely to be sold if the temperature is higher than 38 degrees

docs.title: Check Your Program
docs.text: Your program should use validation for the temperature and should only accept values from 20 to 45 inclusive.

docs.title: Lower Case

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
Write a Python program that inputs a character and checks whether it is lowercase.

Your program should:

  • get the user to enter a character and store it in a suitable variable
  • determine whether the entered character is a lowercase character
  • output LOWER if the user has entered a lowercase character
  • output NOT LOWER if the user has entered any other character

Use meaningful variable names, correct syntax and correct indentation.

docs.title: Check Your Program
docs.text: Test your program with a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a number.

docs.title: Pick A Card
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 3

Save your file as: Pick A Card.py

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
A program is being developed in Python to simulate a card game.

Throughout the game, each player always has 100 cards. Each card displays a number.

Players take it in turns to swap one of their cards with another random card from a set of cards until a player has a run of five numbers in sequence within their 100 cards.

The starter code below gets a player to enter the position of a card to swap.

position = int(input("Enter card position: "))

Extend the program. It should keep getting the user to enter the card position until they enter a card position between 1 and 100 inclusive.

Use meaningful variable names, correct syntax and correct indentation.

docs.title: Check Your Program
docs.text: Test your program with values below 1, above 100 and inside the valid range.

The squared number sequence starts:

1, 4, 9, 16, 25

1, 8, 27, 64

Ask the user:

docs.title: 6th Form Admissions
docs.text:

Save your file as: 6th Form Admissions.py

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
Write a program that calculates whether a pupil has enough GCSE points for sixth form admission.

The program should:

  • asks the user to input how many GCSEs they have
  • allows the user to enter a grade for each GCSE
  • works out how many points they have got, where grade 9 is worth 9, grade 8 is worth 8, and so on

Output rules:

  • if their score is 40 or over, output You can go to the sixth form
  • if their score is between 35 and 39, output A discussion is needed
  • otherwise, output Sorry not enough points.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • use a loop to collect all GCSE grades
  • keep a running total of the score
  • use selection to choose the correct final message

docs.title: Bingo!
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 4

Save your file as: Bingo!.py

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
A program is being written to simulate a computer science revision game in the style of bingo.

At the beginning of the game, a bingo ticket is generated with nine different key terms from computer science in a 3 x 3 grid.

Example bingo ticket:

CPU ALU Pixel NOT gate Binary LAN Register Cache Protocol

The player will be prompted to answer a series of questions. If an answer matches a key term on the player's bingo ticket, the key term will be marked off automatically.

The program uses a two-dimensional array called ticket to represent a bingo ticket.

The program also uses a subroutine called generateKeyTerm. When called, this subroutine returns a random key term, for example CPU, ALU or NOT gate.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Complete the Python program by filling in the five gaps.

Your solution should:

  • use the two-dimensional ticket array
  • call generateKeyTerm when a random key term is needed
  • avoid duplicate terms where possible
  • create a complete 3 x 3 bingo ticket

student1@laurustrust.org.uk

  • contains an @ symbol
  • does not contain any spaces

Your email is acceptable

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
Roger has switched to a new electric supplier.

He will receive free electricity one day a week. He will not pay for the day when he uses the least amount of electricity.

Write a program that:

  • allows the user to input each day of the week
  • allows the user to input the number of electricity units used for each day
  • compares the usage values
  • outputs the day that will be free of charge

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • collect a usage value for each day

Save your file as: How Many Cars.py

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
Write a program that works out whether there are enough car seats for a trip.

The program should:

  • asks the user to input how many cars are available for a trip
  • asks the user to input how many people are going on the trip

docs.title: Logging In
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 4

Save your file as: Logging In.py

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
Write a program that asks a user for a unique ID. It should check the ID against a list of stored IDs.

If the ID matches one in the list, the user will be authorised and a relevant message will display.

If the ID does not match, the user will be asked to enter their ID again. They get three attempts before they are locked out.

You will need to create a list of ten unique IDs. Each ID should contain two letters and four numbers in this format:

SD5545

Example success message:

Hello user SD5545. You have been authorised.

Example lockout message:

ID wrong. You have been locked out.

Each time the user enters the wrong ID, they should be told how many attempts they have left.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • store ten valid IDs in a list
  • allow a maximum of three attempts
  • authorise the user if the ID is found
  • show how many attempts remain after each incorrect ID
  • lock the user out after three failed attempts

OCR Tech is an online shop that sells electronics such as TVs and game consoles.

Customers can use a discount code to reduce the price of their purchase.

Valid discount codes and their value in pounds are stored in a global two-dimensional array with the identifier discount.

docs.title: Pin Checker

Save your file as: Pin Checker.py

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
Write a program that checks how strong a user's PIN number is.

The user should input their PIN number. The program should output whether it is strong. If it is not strong, the program should explain why.

PIN rules:

  • the PIN must be 4 digits long
  • the PIN must not be four consecutive numbers, such as 1234 or 5678

docs.title: Battleships
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 5

Save your file as: Battleships.py

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
A developer wants to simulate a simple version of Battleships.

The ships are located on a one-dimensional array called board.

There are always three ships placed on the board:

  • one carrier that has size three
  • one cruiser that has size two
  • one destroyer that has size one

The size of the board is always 15 squares.

The carrier, for example, might be found at locations board[1], board[2] and board[3].

A player makes a guess to see if a ship, or part of a ship, is located at a particular location. If a ship is found at the location, then the player has hit the ship at this location.

Every value in the board array is 0, 1 or 2:

  • 0 indicates an empty location
  • 1 indicates a ship is at this location and has not been hit
  • 2 indicates a ship is at this location and has been hit

Develop a subroutine that works out how far away the game is from ending.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The subroutine should:

  • have a sensible identifier
  • take the board as a parameter
  • work out and output how many hits have been made
  • work out how many locations containing a ship have not been hit yet
  • output Winner if there are no ship locations left to hit
  • output Almost there if there are 1, 2 or 3 ship locations left to hit

docs.title: Inverse Image
docs.text:
Difficulty: Level 5

Save your file as: Inverse Image.py

docs.title: Brief
docs.text:
A black and white image can be represented as a two-dimensional array where:

  • 0 represents a white pixel
  • 1 represents a black pixel

Two images are exact inverses of each other if:

  • every white pixel in the first image is black in the second image
  • every black pixel in the first image is white in the second image

A developer has started to create an algorithm that compares two 3 x 3 black and white images, image1 and image2, to see if they are exact inverses of each other.

Complete the algorithm so that, when it ends, the value of the variable inverse is True if the two images are inverses of each other, or False if they are not.

The algorithm should work for any 3 x 3 black and white images stored in image1 and image2.

Indexing starts at zero.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Your solution should:

  • compare every position in the two 3 x 3 arrays
  • check that each pair of pixels is opposite
  • set inverse to False if any pair is not opposite
  • leave inverse as True only when every pair matches the inverse rule
